Introduction

Artificial intelligence has become a central object of both technical and social inquiry. Over the past decade, the field has shifted from handcrafted symbolic rules toward data-driven models that learn representations from large corpora; this shift has transformed questions about perception, language, and planning into questions about scaling, evaluation, and alignment. At the same time, the rapid adoption of AI systems has exposed tensions among performance, interpretability, and accountability, making it necessary to frame AI not only as an engineering achievement but also as a regulated practice. The present paper is motivated by a structural observation: modern AI systems are rarely isolated algorithms; they are layered artifacts in which models, data pipelines, evaluation protocols, organizational incentives, and regulatory expectations interact. This layered character can be captured in a deliberately nested notation, ( ( ( ( ( [ { [ (AI) ] } ] ) ) ) ) ), in which the innermost element denotes the model itself, the surrounding brackets and braces denote data, evaluation, and governance constraints, and the outermost parentheses denote the broader institutional context.

We argue that a more satisfactory approach to AI research combines three commitments: formal methods for specifying intended behavior, empirical methods for measuring real-world effects, and governance mechanisms that make responsibility legible across technical, organizational, and legal boundaries. The remainder of this introduction proceeds in three steps. First, we review recent developments in machine learning, large language models, and multimodal systems. Second, we identify the principal limitations of current evaluation regimes, with particular attention to benchmark saturation, distributional shift, and adversarial misuse. Third, we outline the contributions of this paper, including a taxonomy of risks, a method for auditing decision pipelines, and a set of policy-relevant recommendations. By taking these steps, we aim to provide a foundation for research that is both technically rigorous and socially consequential.
